references.text: Jesus took the twelve disciples aside to prepare them for what was about to happen in Jerusalem. Parallel passages are found in Matthew 20:17-19 and Mark 10:32-34, where the same event is described with similar details.

Matthew's parallel account of Jesus' third prediction of his suffering, where he takes the twelve disciples aside on the way up to Jerusalem and tells them about his coming suffering, death, and resurrection.

Mark's parallel account, where Jesus is on his way up to Jerusalem and tells the twelve in detail what will happen to him—being handed over, mocked, spit upon, flogged, and killed, and rising again on the third day.

Isaiah's song of the suffering servant is a central prophecy about the suffering and death of the Son of Man. Jesus refers to how 'all that has been written by the prophets about the Son of Man' will be fulfilled, and Isaiah 53:1-12 is the most detailed Old Testament prophecy concerning the coming Messiah's substitutionary suffering.

Psalm 22:1-19 is a prophetic psalm that describes in detail the Messiah's suffering—mockery, piercing of hands and feet, division of garments—all of which are fulfilled in Jesus' story of suffering in Jerusalem.

After the resurrection, Jesus rebukes the travelers on the road to Emmaus and shows them everything the prophets have said about him: Luke 24:25-27. This confirms that 'all that has been written by the prophets' (18:31) concerns his suffering and glory.

Jesus shows the disciples that all that was written about him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms had to be fulfilled (Luke 24:44-46). This expands on what he said in 18:31, namely that the words of the prophets concerning the Son of Man must come to pass.
Jesus' first prediction of his suffering in Luke: Luke 9:22, where he says that the Son of Man must suffer greatly, be rejected, be killed, and rise again on the third day.

Jesus' second prediction of his suffering in Luke (Luke 9:44-45), where he says that the Son of Man will be handed over into human hands, but the disciples did not understand this saying—just as they also failed to understand it in 18:34.
Hosea 6:1-2 speaks of the Lord making alive after two days and raising up on the third day, which has been understood as a prophetic reference to the resurrection that Jesus here predicts.
Paul explains in Acts 13:27-29 that the people and leaders of Jerusalem fulfilled the words of the prophets when they condemned Jesus—a direct fulfillment of what Jesus predicted in Luke 18:31.
